meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is the mark of a truly intelligent person to be moved by statistics'?
meta.ogDescription: Not George Bernard Shaw. The thought comes from Bertrand Russell’s 1926 book; the polished wording is a later paraphrase, documented by 1994.

answer.label: Not George Bernard Shaw — the thought is Bertrand Russell’s
answer.sourceLine: George Bernard Shaw never wrote this. The idea comes from Bertrand Russell, who in his 1926 book Education and the Good Life wrote that sympathy may “go so far as to enable a man to be moved emotionally by statistics.” The neat modern wording is a paraphrase that evolved over decades and, per Quote Investigator, reached this exact form only around 1994 — Shaw appears to have been substituted for Russell (Bernard for Bertrand) by 1981.

source.heading: The real source
source.excerpt: It may only go so far as sympathy with suffering which is portrayed vividly and touchingly, as in a good novel; it may, on the other hand, go so far as to enable a man to be moved emotionally by statistics. This capacity for abstract sympathy is as rare as it is important.
trail: Origin (1926): Bertrand Russell wrote of sympathy that could “enable a man to be moved emotionally by statistics” in Education and the Good Life — verifiable verbatim in the full Project Gutenberg text.
Drift, then swap: Quote Investigator tracks the line being credited to Russell for years before it was reassigned to George Bernard Shaw by 1981 — likely a Bertrand/Bernard confusion.
Final wording (c. 1994): The exact modern sentence has no basis in Shaw’s works and is first documented around 1994, already attributed to Shaw.
source.excerptNote: Bertrand Russell, Education and the Good Life (1926) — the actual origin of the thought. Note how different this is from the crisp aphorism now pinned on Shaw.

source.rightsNote: The idea traces to Bertrand Russell’s Education and the Good Life (New York: Boni & Liveright, 1926), which is old enough to be public domain in the United States. But the exact sentence shown here is not Russell’s verbatim wording — it is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable author, first documented (and misattributed to Shaw) around 1994, so no clean copyright status can be asserted for it.

author.name: Bertrand Russell
author.heading: About Bertrand Russell
author.bio: Bertrand Russell was a British philosopher, logician and social critic, co-author of Principia Mathematica and winner of the 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature. His 1926 book Education and the Good Life argued that a truly educated mind should be able to feel sympathy even for suffering it knows only through numbers.

misattribution.heading: How Russell became ‘Shaw’
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook magnet-name misattribution: a thoughtful line by one famous Briton drifted onto an even more quotable one.

items.why: Shaw is the name plastered across quote sites, but Quote Investigator finds no such line in his writings; the earliest Shaw credit dates only to 1981, likely a ‘Bertrand’/‘Bernard’ mix-up.
The line has also been pinned on Oscar Wilde, another catch-all wit — with no source in his work either, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine origin is Bertrand Russell, Education and the Good Life (1926), whose line about being “moved emotionally by statistics” you can read verbatim in the full text.

context.heading: Why the line resonates
lead: Russell’s point was moral, not flattering: most people weep at one person’s suffering yet stay unmoved by a death-rate that represents thousands. He thought bridging that gap — feeling numbers as if they were faces — was a rare and vital fruit of real education.
Stripped to a one-liner and handed to Shaw, the thought became a compliment to the clever. The original was a challenge to everyone.
context.pull: “This capacity for abstract sympathy is as rare as it is important.”
